title: Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) (AWS Lake Formation Test Product)
description:
Open this product detail page to access the AWS Open Data version of this data set. This AWS Data Exchange-published product contains a snapshot from the open data set "Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) and Legal Entity Reference Data (LE-RD)" as of November 2022.
The Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) is a 20-character, alpha-numeric code based on the ISO 17442 standard developed by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO). It connects to key reference information that enables clear and unique identification of legal entities participating in financial transactions. Each LEI contains information about an entity’s ownership structure and thus answers the questions of 'who is who’ and ‘who owns whom’. Simply put, the publicly available LEI data pool can be regarded as a global directory, which greatly enhances transparency in the global marketplace. The Financial Stability Board (FSB) has reiterated that global LEI adoption underpins “multiple financial stability objectives” such as improved risk management in firms as well as better assessment of micro and macro prudential risks. As a result, it promotes market integrity while containing market abuse and financial fraud. Last but not least, LEI rollout “supports higher quality and accuracy of financial data overall”. The publicly available LEI data pool is a unique key to standardized information on legal entities globally. The data is registered and regularly verified according to protocols and procedures established by the Regulatory Oversight Committee. In cooperation with its partners in the Global LEI System, the Global Legal Entity Identifier Foundation (GLEIF) continues to focus on further optimizing the quality, reliability and usability of LEI data, empowering market participants to benefit from the wealth of information available with the LEI population. The drivers of the LEI initiative, i.e. the Group of 20, the FSB and many regulators around the world, have emphasized the need to make the LEI a broad public good. The Global LEI Index, made available by GLEIF, greatly contributes to meeting this objective. It puts the complete LEI data at the disposal of any interested party, conveniently and free of charge. The benefits for the wider business community to be generated with the Global LEI Index grow in line with the rate of LEI adoption. To maximize the benefits of entity identification across financial markets and beyond, firms are therefore encouraged to engage in the process and get their own LEI. Obtaining an LEI is easy. Registrants simply contact their preferred business partner from the list of LEI issuing organizations available on the GLEIF website.

description:
Market.us announces publication of its most recently generated research report titled, “Global Frankincense Essential Oil Market 
by Grade Type (<85%, 85%-90%, 90%-95%, >95%), By Application (Research uses, Drug Formula, Dietic Foods, Cosmetics, Other) and by Region – Global Forecast to 2028.”, Which offers a holistic view of the global frankincense essential oil market through systematic segmentation that covers every aspect of the target market.
The global frankincense essential oil market is projected to be US$ 193.4 Mn in 2018 to reach US$ 406.1 Mn by 2028 at a CAGR of 7.7%.
Frankincense is produced from hardy Boswellia trees, by slashing the barks and allowing the resin to harden. The traditional medicine is believed to have several properties including anti-inflammatory, expectorant, antiseptic, and even anxiolytic and anti-neurotic effect. It is primarily found in India and Pakistan and very few parts of Yemen and Oman. The word Frankincense arises from the French word “franc-encens” – meaning – quality incense. It is used for its various applications like medicinal, spiritual and cosmetics. Frankincense essential oil is used for fragrance applications, as well as for perfumery applications. It is obtained by a steam distillation process where the tree resin is used. Frankincense oil smells fresher as well as sweeter, which also finds applications in air fresheners. It is also used in pharmaceuticals industries in large scale. However, it is harmful to when consumed without proper dilution.
Frankincense comes in several grades, and its quality is based on colour, purity, aroma, and age. Silver and Hojari are the uppermost grades of frankincense. Frankincense resin is eatable and frequently used in many traditional medicines in Asia for healthy skin and digestion. For internal consumption, edible frankincense must be pure, and it should be translucent without any black or brown impurities. It is light yellow with a (very) slight greenish tint. title: Container Port Traffic (TEU) | World Bank Open Data
description:
Port container traffic measures the flow of containers from land to sea transport modes., and vice versa, in twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs), a standard-size container. Data refer to coastal shipping as well as international journeys. Transshipment traffic is counted as two lifts at the intermediate port (once to off-load and again as an outbound lift) and includes empty units. TEU is the standard unit, referring to 20-foot equivalent units or 20-foot-long cargo container. The size of cargo containers range from 20 feet long to more than 50 feet long. The international measure is the smallest box, the 20-footer or 20-foot-equivalent unit (TEU). This release contains container port traffic (TEU: 20 foot equivalent units) for all countries in the world.
The original publisher of this data is The World Bank. This content is published as World Bank Open Data and provides free and open access to global development data. This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC-BY 4.0). This data is anonymized/aggregated.

(Please note that you will need IAM permissions for CloudFormation, AWS Data Exchange, IAM, Lambda, Glue, Athena and QuickSight, in order to deploy the CloudFormation template.)
Under the product listing, scroll down to Data sets section and click on the Data set name
Under the Revisions section, click on the most recent revision
Under Assets, checkmark container-port-traffic/automation/post-processing-code.zip and click Export to S3
Choose the S3 Bucket where you would like to store the dataset. Make sure you only choose the S3 bucket. The asset comes with a pre-defined directory structure
Under Assets, checkmark container-port-traffic/automation/cloudformation.yaml and click either Export to S3 or Export to computer
If you exported the cloudformation.yaml to S3, go to the S3 UI on the AWS console and navigate to the location where the cloudformation.yaml is stored. In S3, click on the cloudformation.yaml and copy the url from the Object URL
Now, from your AWS Management Console, log onto Amazon CloudFormation UI and click Create Stack
Under Choose a template either provide the template via uploading from local computer or specify the S3 object url and click Next
Provide a friendly stack name in the Stack name text box
In the SourceS3Bucket field, input the S3 bucket name that you chose earlier to store the container-port-traffic/automation/post-processing-code.zip file
Leave rest of the fields as is
Click Next
In the Options screen, click Next
Tick mark the I acknowledge that AWS CloudFormation might create IAM resources. box
Click Create

Lambda function to setup automatic AWS Data Exchange revision updates for this dataset
CloudWatch Event rule that will automatically trigger the Lambda function every time a new revision update is published

Necessary IAM roles and permissions

Main Overview
The G.19 Statistical Release, "Consumer Credit," reports outstanding credit extended to individuals for household, family, and other personal expenditures, excluding loans secured by real estate.
Total consumer credit comprises two major types: revolving and nonrevolving. Revolving credit plans may be unsecured or secured by collateral and allow a consumer to borrow up to a prearranged limit and repay the debt in one or more installments. Credit card loans comprise most of revolving consumer credit measured in the G.19, but other types, such as prearranged overdraft plans, are also included. Nonrevolving credit is closed-end credit extended to consumers that is repaid on a prearranged repayment schedule and may be secured or unsecured. To borrow additional funds, the consumer must enter into an additional contract with the lender. Consumer motor vehicle and education loans comprise the majority of nonrevolving credit, but other loan types, such as boat loans, recreational vehicle loans, and personal loans, are also included.
The G.19 also reports selected terms of credit, including interest rates on new car loans, personal loans, and credit card plans at commercial banks. Historically, the G.19 also included series that measure the terms of credit for motor vehicle loans at finance companies.

title: OpenFEMA Dataset: Disaster Declarations Summaries - V2 | FEMA
description:
The source code outlining how this product gathers, transforms, revises and publishes its datasets is available at https://github.com/rearc-data/fema-disaster-declarations-summaries 
.
Main Overview
FEMA Disaster Declarations Summary is a summarized dataset describing all federally declared disasters. This dataset lists all official FEMA Disaster Declarations, beginning with the first disaster declaration in 1953 and features all three disaster declaration types: major disaster, emergency, and fire management assistance. The dataset includes declared recovery programs and geographic areas (county not available before 1964; Fire Management records are considered partial due to historical nature of the dataset).
Please note the unique structure of the disaster sequencing (due to a numbering system that originated in the 1950's-1970's):
0001-1999 Major Disaster Declaration
2000-2999 Fire Management
3000-3999 Emergency Declaration (Special Emergency)
4000- Major Disaster Declaration
This is raw, unedited data from FEMA's National Emergency Management Information System (NEMIS) and as such is subject to a small percentage of human error. The dataset is primarily composed of historical data that was manually entered into NEMIS after it launched in 1998. The financial information is derived from NEMIS and not FEMA's official financial systems.
Due to differences in reporting periods, status of obligations, and how business rules are applied, this financial information may differ slightly from official publication on public websites such as usaspending.gov. This dataset is not intended to be used for any official federal financial reporting.
Data Source
The included datasets are provided in CSV, JSON and JSONA formats. The data contains the following data fields:
Name Title Type Description
femaDeclarationString FEMA Declaration String string Agency standard method for uniquely identifying Stafford Act declarations - Concatenation of declaration type, disaster number and state code. Ex: DR-4393-NC.
disasterNumber Disaster Number number Sequentially assigned number used to designate an event or incident declared as a disaster.
state State string The name or phrase describing the U.S. state, district, or territory.
declarationType Declaration Type string Two character code that defines if this is a major disaster, fire management, or emergency declaration.
declarationDate Declaration Date date Date the disaster was declared.
fyDeclared FY Declared number Fiscal year in which the disaster was declared.
incidentType Incident Type string Type of incident such as fire or flood. The incident type will affect the types of assistance available.
declarationTitle Declaration Title string Title for the disaster.
ihProgramDeclared IH Program Declared boolean Denotes whether the Individuals and Households program was declared for this disaster.
iaProgramDeclared IA Program Declared boolean Denotes whether the Individual Assistance program was declared for this disaster.
paProgramDeclared PA Program Declared boolean Denotes whether the Public Assistance program was declared for this disaster.
hmProgramDeclared HM Program Declared boolean Denotes whether the Hazard Mitigation program was declared for this disaster.
incidentBeginDate Incident Begin Date date Date the incident itself began.
incidentEndDate Incident End Date date Date the incident itself ended.
disasterCloseoutDate Disaster Closeout Date date Date all financial transactions for all programs are completed.
fipsStateCode FIPS State Code string FIPS two-digit numeric code used to identify the United States, the District of Columbia, US territories, outlying areas of the US and freely associated states.
fipsCountyCode FIPS County Code string FIPS three-digit numeric code used to identify counties and county equivalents in the United States, the District of Columbia, US territories, outlying areas of the US and freely associated states.
placeCode Place Code string A unique code system FEMA uses internally to recognize locations that takes the numbers '99' + the 3-digit county FIPS code. There are some declared locations that don't have recognized FIPS county codes in which case we assigned a unique identifier.
designatedArea Designated Area string The name or phrase describing the U.S. county that was included in the declaration.
declarationRequestNumber Declaration Request Number string Unique ID assigned to request for a disaster declaration.
lastRefresh Last Refresh date Date the record was last updated in the API data store.
hash Hash string MD5 Hash of the fields and values of the record.
id ID string Unique ID assigned to the record.
To learn about about the data fields, please visit the dataset's documentation 
on FEMA's website.

title: Federal Reserve | Household Debt Service & Financial Obligations Ratios
description:
The source code outlining how this product gathers, transforms, revises and publishes its datasets is available at https://github.com/rearc-data/federal-reserve-household-debt-financial-obligations 
.
Main Overview
The household Debt Service Ratio (DSR) is the ratio of total required household debt payments to total disposable income.
The DSR is divided into two parts. The Mortgage DSR is total quarterly required mortgage payments divided by total quarterly disposable personal income. The Consumer DSR is total quarterly scheduled consumer debt payments divided by total quarterly disposable personal income. The Mortgage DSR and the Consumer DSR sum to the DSR.
Quarterly values for the Debt Service Ratio are available from 1980 forward.
The Financial Obligations Ratio is a broader measure than the Debt Service Ratio. It includes rent payments on tenant-occupied property, auto lease payments, homeowners' insurance, and property tax payments. These statistics are obtained from the National Income and Product Accounts 
.
Data Source
The dataset included with this resource is presented in CSV, XLS and XML formats. The data files include the following data fields:
Series Description (Time Period, e.g. "2017Q2")
Debt service ratio, seasonally adjusted (Percent)
Mortgage debt service ratio, seasonally adjusted (Percent)
Consumer debt service ratio, seasonally adjusted (Percent)
Financial obligations ratio, seasonally adjusted (Percent)

title: ESG News Sentiment Scores Dataset (Large Cap) - Trial Product
description:
ESG News Sentiment Scores Dataset - Trial
Amenity Analytics has created an ESG dataset that provides company and sector-level analysis of hundreds of news sources for monitoring and tracking ESG issues in-depth.
This trial dataset is an industrial-scale contextual NLP applied to thousands of news sources to develop in-depth, real-time scoring at the company level on ESG issues relating to companies globally. This dataset excludes companies with fewer than one result per day, leaving 1,227 of the largest public US companies to examine. Our sources comprehensively include top international, national, regional, local, and business news along with additional Amenity identified high quality sources. The dataset tracks daily ESG extractions from January 2018 to June 2021.
The Amenity ESG language model employs contextual analysis and language patterns to provide investors with real-time, broadly aggregated, and unbiased environmental-, social- and governance-related evidence and scores. Amenity’s taxonomy consists of 22 events across three dimensions (E, S, and G). These events can be viewed in sum to represent the ESG profile of a given company or analyzed individually. Our approach considers the sentiment, event, and materiality to the company described in the text.
Amenity applies natural language processing and sentiment analysis on news to derive a numerical score (signal). The score is the result of the net sentiment divided by the total negative and positive extractions in the transcript, and per ESG topic. Also includes counts that make up those scores.
The Values in this dataset are represented with scores between -1 and 1. A score of -1 is the most negative and +1 is the most positive. Neutral is 0.
The dataset includes total score + counts and score + counts per key driver (Governance, General, Social and Environmental).
Key Benefits
Systematically evaluate and quantify the materiality of Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) factors in the news on companies in your investment universe.
Unbiased and transparent data. Our ESG model employs contextual analysis and language patterns to capture and analyze all critical events across a rich dataset of thousands of news sources providing investors broadly aggregated and unbiased E, S, and G-related evidence and scores.

Via Marketplace: Signal file or dashboard interface. Dashboard features an intuitive user interface that applies an ESG lens to companies within your investment universe. Create sentiment summaries, or segment baskets of equities based on distinct ESG profiles.

title: 2019 Antarctica Circumnavigation - SD-1022 Complete Data Set
description:
A saildrone is an unmanned surface vehicle (USV) that combines wind-powered propulsion technology and solar-powered meteorological and oceanographic sensors to perform autonomous long-range data collection missions in the harshest ocean environments.
This data set was collected from the first Saildrone Antarctic Circumnavigation. A fleet of 3 Saildrone unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) were launched from Bluff, New Zealand on January 19, 2019. SD-1022 and SD-1023 were damaged in the first 24 hours of the mission in winds gusting over 50 knots and 20 foot waves. They returned to New Zealand for servicing and were relaunched on May 10, 2019 with ruggedized wings. SD-1022 was recovered in South Africa on September 20, 2019 after sustaining damage in a storm.
SD-1022 was outfit with a Simrad WBT EK80 mini transceiver and transducer as well as the standard Saildrone metocean sensor suite 
. Its mission objectives were to collect acoustic backscatter data for krill and biomass studies and also to collect oceanographic and atmospheric data from the Southern Ocean.
This is a complete collection of data collected by SD-1022 while it was deployed from May 8, 2019 until September 20, 2019, which includes:
Acoustic data: Raw EK80 backscatter data, and EK80 calibration data from SD-1022's 2018 mission in the Arctic for NOAA Fisheries 
Environmental data in a CF-compliant netCDF file collected from metocean sensors and USV telemetry transmitted in near realtime in 1-minute time-averaged resolution for the duration of the mission
Raw environmental data in CF-compliant netCDF files collected from metocean sensors stored onboard the vehicle through the duration of the mission in 1-hz resolution in 24-hour files
Raw wind data in CF-compliant netCDF files from the sonic anemometer and USV telemetry stored onboard the vehicle through the duration of the mission in 20-hz resolution in 24-hour files

title: Vegetation Indices Maps
description:
D-CAT Vegetation Indices Data Product Overview
This data product provides a time series of ten different Vegetation Indices maps of areas in Argentina and Ukraine across a number of dates in 2019 and 2020. The indices provided here are valuable in many land monitoring contexts important to sustainability and resource monitoring including agriculture, forestry and many others. Each index is explained in more detail along with how it is best interpreted and how it is used in agricultural management. The ten Vegetation Indices offered in this sample product are: NDVI, LAI, PSRI, RGRI, EVI, GVI, MTVI2, OSAVI, RDVI, RENDVI. An RGB image is provided as well.
The data provided here is a satellite remote sensing derived product using the European Space Agency Sentinel 2 multispectral satellite data atmospherically corrected using the Sen2cor algorithm.
 Use Cases
The availability of a time series of Vegetation Indices contributes significantly to the creation of bespoke analytics models that can improve the following: vegetation health monitoring, land use and land use change (LULC) monitoring, crop classification, yield prediction, biomass estimation, forest fire monitoring.
The applicability of these Vegetation Indices can be specific to species, vegetation types and local conditions. The various Vegetation Indices can provide important information to enhance area-scale and field assessment of different vegetation and agronomic measures. They can be utilised to assess various plant parameters, e.g. leaf area, ground cover, biomass, leaf chlorophyll content, residue cover. Evaluation of vegetation, forestry and agricultural decisions can be constructed around utilising the spatial and temporal variation of Vegetation Indices across fields or other areas of interest.
 Overview - Spectral indices
Optical imagery, i.e. pictures taken with cameras, which collect light focused by a lens, can be collected at different wavelengths within the possible range of wavelengths available (think of the colours of a rainbow).
Analysis of imagery of the same place captured at different wavelengths can reveal a lot about the content of the scene being viewed. When comparisons are made of scene content at different wavelengths Spectral Indices are the most common form of spectral image enhancement and there are indices that support a broad range of applications, from minerals to soil to vegetation. For example, plants reflect light much more towards the end of the visible spectrum and beyond, and by analysing the steepness and magnitude of the rise in reflectance, the amount of chlorophyll, which is an indication of vegetation greenness can be quantified. A Spectral Index is the name given to any numerical ratio or metric that reveals some particular aspect of information about the scene using two or more of the available images at different wavelengths.
The satellite images used by this D-CAT data product capture optical images of the same scene at 12 different wavelengths. We then apply a series of processes to those satellite images to produce what are called Vegetation Indices. These are Spectral Indices which focus on aspects of the data relevant to vegetation and agricultural applications.
All Spectral Indices, including the ten Vegetation Indices provided in this data product, are dimensionless quantities and the file images give the Vegetation Indices for each pixel imaged, i.e. the 10m2 patch of ground covered by the satellite.
 Overview - Vegetation Indices
Vegetation Indices are measures of vegetation activity and have been widely shown to vary with the seasonal variability of green foliage and the space between growing plants. A number of different Vegetation Indices have been developed and their variability shows that each was developed to enhance a specific canopy reflectance parameter (sunlight reflected from a surface) or to minimise the effects of the atmosphere and soil. The ten Vegetation Indices offered in this sample data product have been selected for their proven applicability in monitoring vegetation. They include: NDVI, LAI, PSRI, RGRI, EVI, GVI, MTVI2, OSAVI, RDVI, RENDVI. Also included is an RGB image of each satellite observation.
Each of the ten Vegetation Indices is now explained in more detail along with how it is best interpreted and how it is used by some practitioners to assist vegetation and agricultural management, monitoring and prediction.
 NDVI
Normalised Difference Vegetation index (NDVI) is a measure of live green vegetation. It is a widely used VI that helps identify areas of vegetation and their “condition”.
VALUE RANGE: -1 to 1
 Observation Typical Values
Thick vegetation 0.5 to 1
Medium vegetation 0.14 to 0.5
Scarce vegetation 0.09 to 0.14
Bare ground 0.025 to 0.090
Clouds 0.002 to 0.025
Ice and snow -0.046 to 0.002
Water -1 to 0.046
NDVI has limitations, creating the need for other specialised Vegetation Indices. It is sensitive to a number of factors that can alter its value, including:  
Atmospheric effects: For satellite imagery, the composition of the atmosphere, in particular water vapour and aerosols, can significantly affect the measurements made in space. This D-CAT data product corrects for this by adding an essential quality step that processes the atmospheric effects out of the image before NDVI is calculated.  
Soil effects: Soils tend to darken when wet, and so the amount of light reflected is a function of water content. This can have the effect that the NDVI of an area can appear to change as a result of soil moisture changes and not because of vegetation changes.  
Saturation effect: NDVI can saturate (values close to 1) in dense vegetation.
LAI
Leaf Area Index (LAI) is a reference tool for crop growth and is a widely used measurement for describing plant canopy structure.
LAI is generated using spectral images and estimates the ratio of leaf canopy to ground area, and is therefore a useful metric for describing both spatial and temporal patterns of canopy growth and productivity. Like all Vegetation Indices, it is a dimensionless measure because it is a ratio – in this case of areas.
Values can be highly variable, with some desert ecosystems having an LAI of less than 1, while the densest tropical forests can have an LAI as high as 9. Seasonally, annual and deciduous canopies and croplands can exhibit large variations in LAI. For example, from seeding to maturity, maize LAI can range from 0 to 6. As such, LAI is a useful metric for describing both spatial and temporal patterns of canopy growth and productivity.
VALUE RANGE: 0 to 9
TYPICAL VALUES: 0 to 6, where values up to 2 are generally little / low vegetation. Mid-latitude forests and shrubland typically have LAI values between 3 and 6.
PSRI
Plant Senescence Reflectance Index (PSRI) indicates and quantifies the ageing process of vegetation. As vegetation begins to age, chlorophyll degradation starts to reveal the carotenoids and this depletion is exploited by the PSRI to indicate the level of plant ageing. A visible outward sign to the human eye is the leaf colour change observed in Autumn months. An increase in PSRI indicates increased canopy stress (carotenoid pigment), the onset of canopy senescence and plant fruit ripening.
This index finds application for a variety of agricultural purposes, including vegetation health monitoring, plant physiological stress detection, crop production and yield analysis.
VALUE RANGE: -1 to 1
TYPICAL VALUES: -0.1 to 0.5 for green vegetation.
RGRI
The Red Green Ratio index (RGRI) indicates relative leaf redness.
The index is therefore useful as an indicator of leaf production or plant stress, and can also be used also indicate flowering in some canopies.
Redness is caused by anthocyanins in the vegetation, which tend to be more abundant in fruits and flowers than crops, except for those of colour (e.g. red cabbage). By examining the spectral images the relative abundance of anthocyanin to chlorophyll is indicated, providing what can be a beneficial tool for phenology (the study of the crop growth cycle). Advantages of RGRI as a phenological indicator have been reported as including: Site-independent detection of the early phase of leaf green-up and the middle phase of autumn colouring. A distinct response to subtle disturbance and the difference of ecosystem types. Provides early indication of flowering rapeseed (canola) Valuable in monitoring viticulture Applications also extend to canopy stress detection, and crop yield prediction.
VALUE RANGE: 0.1 to 15
TYPICAL VALUES: 0.7 to 3 for green vegetation
EVI
The Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI) is complementary to NDVI as another tool for analysing vegetation growth.
Specific features include:
The vegetation signal is enhanced, which assists analysis. Improved sensitivity in high biomass regions. Improved vegetation monitoring due to independence from the background signal of the canopy and reduced sensitivity to atmospheric effects (weather). The index does not become saturated as easily as NDVI when viewing areas with large amounts of chlorophyll.
Whereas NDVI is chlorophyll sensitive, EVI is more responsive to canopy structural variations, including the leaf area index (LAI), canopy type, plant physiognomy and canopy architecture.
VALUE RANGE: 0 to 1
TYPICAL VALUES: 0.20 to 0.80 for healthy vegetation.
GVI
The Green Vegetation Index (GVI) is another broadband greenness measure to use alongside NDVI and EVI.
However, GVI is more robust to variations in soil than those indices because it separates out the green vegetation from the variation caused by underlying soils or water.
The GVI images can be used to assess vegetation abundance, status and variation across the field, from bare soil to dense canopy. In addition, the GVI can correlate to industry-standard vegetation measures such as Green Leaf Area Index, plant height, biomass or percentage canopy cover for more detailed analysis.
The index has also been claimed to aid in the detection of plant senescence (of interest for stress monitoring and close to harvest) and in identifying potential issues with nitrogen and water uptake by the vegetation.
VALUE RANGE: -1 to 1
TYPICAL VALUES: 0.20 to 0.80 for healthy vegetation.
MTVI2
The Modified Triangular Vegetation Index – Improved (MTVI2) is complementary to LAI.
The index is recognised as a better predictor of green LAI for dense vegetation and is more sensitive than LAI to small changes in vegetation health.
The use of “triangular” in the name is because this index, like the original MTVI on which it is based, is calculated as the area of a hypothetical triangle in spectral space that connects the green peak reflectance, the minimum chlorophyll absorption, and the near infrared (NIR) “shoulder” of the vegetation’s spectral response. The area of the triangle increases when chlorophyll absorption causes a decrease in red reflectance and leaf abundance increases NIR reflectance, indicating increased foliage.
MTVI2 is a “narrowband” index and hence more sensitive to changes.
VALUE RANGE: -1 to 1
TYPICAL VALUES: 0.4 to 0.8 for green vegetation.
OSAVI
The Optimised Soil Adjusted Vegetation Index (OSAVI) is another tool which complements NDVI.
It compensates for NDVI’s limitations when exposed to varying soil colour, soil moisture and saturation effects from high-density vegetation.
OSAVI is therefore best used in areas with relatively sparse vegetation where soil is visible through the canopy.
VALUE RANGE: -1 to 1
TYPICAL VALUES: 0.4 to 0.8 for green vegetation.
RDVI
The Renormalised Difference Vegetation Index (RDVI) is similar to NDVI, but is best employed in the analysis of tall crops with good spacing between rows. This index is similar to OSAVI in that it suppresses the effects of soil and sun, but it should be noted that it does not work well in sparsely vegetated dry areas.
VALUE RANGE: -1 to 1
TYPICAL VALUES: 0.4 to 0.8 for green vegetation.
RENDVI
The Red Edge Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (RENDVI) is a modified NDVI optimised for small changes.
Those small changes can be in canopy foliage content, gap fraction or senescence and the result is an index that can be used in conjunction with, or as an alternative to, NDVI. As a narrowband greenness Vegetation Index, RENDVI is sensitive to factors including the combined effects of foliage chlorophyll concentration, canopy leaf area, foliage clumping and canopy architecture.
VALUE RANGE: -1 to 1
TYPICAL VALUES: 0.4 to 0.8 for green vegetation.
RGB
Red Green Blue (RGB) image showing the True Colour Image (TCI) of the observation.
 Metadata
There are 17 unique satellite observations within this data set. 9 of these are observations of Argentina and 8 are observations of Ukraine. Observations were taken in 2019 and 2020.
There are 22 files associated with each observation:

NUTS for the territorial level: the NUTS (Nomenclature des Unités territoriales Statistiques) classification is standardised across all EU countries to enable cross-country comparison.
NACE for the economic sector: the NACE (Statistical Classification of Economic Activities in the European Community) taxonomy is the classification of economic activities or industries in the European Union.
ISCED for educational levels: the ISCED (International Standard Classification of Education) taxonomy provides a comprehensive framework for organising education programmes and qualifications by applying uniform and internationally agreed on definitions to facilitate comparisons of education systems across countries.
ESCO (European Skills, Competences, Qualifications and Occupations) for occupations and skills: ESCO taxonomy identifies and categorises skills/competencies, qualifications, and occupations relevant for the EU labour market and education and training, in 25 European languages. Below is a brief outline of the three key trends that are fostering global demand for minoxidil market:
1. Rising instances of hair loss caused by air pollution:
Recent studies checking the overall health impact of dust and fuel particles on human scalp have found that air pollution can, among other health concerns, cause hair loss from longer exposure. Researchers discovered that when exposed to some of the most common air pollutants human hair sees a decrease in four key hair protein levels, including CDK2, beta-catenin, cyclin E, and cyclin D1. These proteins are directly responsible for the retention as well as growth of hair among humans.
The study further found that the effect of air pollution on hair health increased when the volume of the airborne particles increased – effectively suggesting that people living in urban areas or in proximity to industrial areas have a higher risk of going bald.
Minoxidil addresses the effects of onset hair loss by reversing the miniaturisation of hair follicles, increasing blood flow to the scalp, and stimulating follicle movement to the growth phase.

2. Growing cases of alopecia across the globe:
According to the National Alopecia Areata Foundation, approximately 2% of the world’s population will develop alopecia areata at one point in their lifetime. What does that mean? The foundation estimates that over 6.7 million people in the US will get alopecia at some point and currently about 700,000 people across the US are living with the condition.
While alopecia areata can start in patients at any age, most people develop the disease during the early stages of their life. In fact, more than 80% of individuals show signs of the ailment before hitting the age of 40, while 40% start showing symptoms by the age of 20. Topical application of minoxidil solution is one of the only solutions to induce hair regrowth in patients with alopecia.
3. Increasing disease burden of hypertension worldwide:
Hypertension is regarded as one of the leading causes of death worldwide, being responsible for more than 12.8% of deaths annually, which translates to 7.5 million lives. Over the past three decades, the overall number of people aged 30 years - 79 years with hypertension has effectively doubled to reach 1.28 billion worldwide. A recent WHO study found that that over half of the patients suffering from hypertension, 62% of men and 53% of women, or a total 720 million people, lack access to the treatment they need.
Among patients with resistant hypertension where multidrug regimen-based therapy has failed, minoxidil has shown to be capable of lowering blood pressure.

Who can access to the Lightcast dataset?

Additional Product information:
After being extracted, job postings are processed and classified into standard statistical classifications:
NUTS for the territorial level: the NUTS (Nomenclature des Unités territoriales Statistiques) classification is standardised across all EU countries to enable cross-country comparison.
NACE for the economic sector: the NACE (Statistical Classification of Economic Activities in the European Community) taxonomy is the classification of economic activities or industries in the European Union.
ISCED for educational levels: the ISCED (International Standard Classification of Education) taxonomy provides a comprehensive framework for organising education programmes and qualifications by applying uniform and internationally agreed on definitions to facilitate comparisons of education systems across countries.
ESCO (European Skills, Competences, Qualifications and Occupations) for occupations and skills: ESCO taxonomy identifies and categorises skills/competencies, qualifications, and occupations relevant for the EU labour market and education and training, in 25 European languages. It was built to provide a common language to help job seekers find jobs that match their skills, connect employment and education providers, and connect labour markets across the European Union. The ESCO Occupation taxonomy covers 436 unique occupations.

title: Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) (AWS Lake Formation Test Product)
description:
Open this product detail page to access the AWS Open Data version of this data set. This AWS Data Exchange-published product contains a snapshot from the open data set "Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) and Legal Entity Reference Data (LE-RD)" as of November 2022.
The Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) is a 20-character, alpha-numeric code based on the ISO 17442 standard developed by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO). It connects to key reference information that enables clear and unique identification of legal entities participating in financial transactions. Each LEI contains information about an entity’s ownership structure and thus answers the questions of 'who is who’ and ‘who owns whom’. Simply put, the publicly available LEI data pool can be regarded as a global directory, which greatly enhances transparency in the global marketplace. The Financial Stability Board (FSB) has reiterated that global LEI adoption underpins “multiple financial stability objectives” such as improved risk management in firms as well as better assessment of micro and macro prudential risks. As a result, it promotes market integrity while containing market abuse and financial fraud. Last but not least, LEI rollout “supports higher quality and accuracy of financial data overall”. The publicly available LEI data pool is a unique key to standardized information on legal entities globally. The data is registered and regularly verified according to protocols and procedures established by the Regulatory Oversight Committee. In cooperation with its partners in the Global LEI System, the Global Legal Entity Identifier Foundation (GLEIF) continues to focus on further optimizing the quality, reliability and usability of LEI data, empowering market participants to benefit from the wealth of information available with the LEI population. The drivers of the LEI initiative, i.e. the Group of 20, the FSB and many regulators around the world, have emphasized the need to make the LEI a broad public good. The Global LEI Index, made available by GLEIF, greatly contributes to meeting this objective. It puts the complete LEI data at the disposal of any interested party, conveniently and free of charge. The benefits for the wider business community to be generated with the Global LEI Index grow in line with the rate of LEI adoption. To maximize the benefits of entity identification across financial markets and beyond, firms are therefore encouraged to engage in the process and get their own LEI. Obtaining an LEI is easy. Registrants simply contact their preferred business partner from the list of LEI issuing organizations available on the GLEIF website.

title: Soil Mineral Indices Maps
description:
D-CAT Soil Mineral Indices Data Product Overview
Soil is a complex material that is extremely variable in its physical and chemical composition. It consists of weathered rocks of the earth’s crust and is continuously evolving and changing. The upper layer is the most important part, containing plant litter, water, roots, micro and macro fauna, and minerals that are formed in situ or transferred to the area by runoff, dust storms, or human activity. The soil surface is exposed to satellite remote sensing, providing an invaluable tool for determining and mapping soil properties.
This product provides a time series of three different Soil Mineral Indices maps of areas in Argentina and Ukraine across a number of dates in 2019 and 2020. The three Soil Mineral Indices provided are: Clay Minerals (CM), Ferrous Minerals (FM) and Iron Oxide (IO). An RGB image is also provided. Each index is explained in more detail along with how they are best interpreted and how they are used in agricultural management. The data provided here is a satellite remote sensing derived product using the European Space Agency Sentinel 2 multispectral satellite data atmospherically corrected using the Sen2cor algorithm.
 Use Cases
The availability of a time series of Soil Mineral Indices contributes significantly to the creation of bespoke analytics models that can improve real insights to support sustainability through soil health monitoring, crop classification, yield prediction and biomass estimation.
Soil mineralogy is an important factor in determining soil properties, quality, and crop growth potential, and is extensively used as a diagnostic criterion in comprehensive soil classification. The most common minerals in soils, quartz, clay minerals, and carbonates, have fundamental spectral features that can be observed by multispectral satellite remote sensing.
If you want to develop private products using these Soil Mineral Indices, reach out to D-CAT and use the Data Exchange for delivery.  
Overview - Spectral indices
Optical imagery, i.e. pictures taken with cameras, which collect light focused by a lens, can be collected at different wavelengths within the possible range of wavelengths available (think of the colours of a rainbow).
Analysis of imagery of the same place captured at different wavelengths can reveal a lot about the content of the scene being viewed. When comparisons are made of scene content at different wavelengths, Spectral Indices are the most common form of spectral image enhancement and there are indices that support a broad range of applications, from minerals and vegetation through to soil. A Spectral Index is the name given to any numerical ratio or metric that reveals some particular aspect of information about the scene using two or more of the available images at different wavelengths.
The satellite images used by D-CAT capture optical images of the same scene at 12 different wavelengths. We then further process those satellite images to produce a range of different Spectral Indices.
All Spectral Indices are dimensionless quantities and the file images provided in this product give the index value for each pixel imaged, i.e. the 10 square metre patch of ground covered by the satellite.
 Soil Mineral Indices
A number of different Soil Mineral Indices have been developed to provide important variables for mineral mapping that assists in identifying the dominant minerals. The three Soil Mineral Indices offered in this data product, Clay Minerals, Ferrous Metals and Iron Oxide, have been selected for their proven applicability in monitoring soil in an agriculture context. Also included is an RGB 'true colour' image of each satellite observation.
Each soil index is now explained in more detail. Each one adds valuable insights that assist sustainability assessments of soil for agricultural management and monitoring.
 Clay Minerals (CM)
The CM index indicates the presence of clay minerals in the soil being imaged.
This index indicates clay minerals, not clay. Clay minerals are hydrous aluminum phyllosilicates that may also contain iron, magnesium, alkali metals and alkaline earths in varying quantities, and are commonly found in fine-grained sedimentary rocks (e.g. shale) and fine-grained metamorphic rocks (e.g. slate). They act as chemical “sponges” by holding water and dissolved plant nutrients, and form an important proportion of the mineral component of soil. Ideally, soil has four components: mineral; organic matter; water; and air. “Good” agricultural soil would have ~45% mineral, ~5% organic matter, ~25% water and ~25% air, with the mineral component comprising equal amounts of sand, silt and clay (termed “loam”).
This index aids soil health management.
VALUE RANGE: 0 to 5
TYPICAL VALUES: Anywhere in the available range depending on abundance
Ferrous Minerals (FM)
The FM index indicates the presence of iron-bearing minerals in the soil being imaged.
Ferrous minerals are the minerals having iron (Fe) as an element in the composition. The amount of iron in different minerals varies, with some being suited to agricultural purposes (e.g. Ferrous Sulphate), and hence the inclusion of this index within this sample data product.
VALUE RANGE: 0 to 10
TYPICAL VALUES: Anywhere in the available range depending on abundance
Iron Oxide (IO)
The Iron Oxide index highlights the presence of iron oxides when exposed ground is imaged.
Iron plays a vital role in the structure and fabric of a soil, as well as soil fertility and plant development. It can be present at high quantities in soils, but its availability to plants is usually very low, and therefore iron deficiency is a common problem. Plants uptake iron in its oxidized forms, Fe2+ (ferrous form) or Fe3+ (ferric form).
This index provides another tool to assist farm management by indicating the presence of iron oxides in soil, such as hematite, goethite and magnetite.
VALUE RANGE: 0 to 10
TYPICAL VALUES: Anywhere in the available range depending on abundance
RGB
Red Green Blue (RGB) image showing the True Colour Image (TCI) of the observation.
 Metadata
There are 17 unique satellite observations within this data set. 9 of these are observations of Argentina and 8 are observations of Ukraine. Observations were taken in 2019 and 2020.
There are 8 files associated with each observation:
CM data (.tif) - A GeoTIFF giving Clay Minerals (CM) values at a 20m resolution but has been upsampled from 20m to 10m to align with the 10m GeoTiffs.
CM preview (.jpg) - A pseudocolour CM JPEG image. Available to view before processing CM data.
FM data (.tif) - A GeoTIFF giving Ferrous Minerals (FM) values at a 10m resolution.
FM preview (.jpg) - A pseudocolour FM JPEG image. Available to view before processing FM data.
IO data (.tif) - A GeoTIFF giving Iron Oxide (IO) values at a 10m resolution.
IO preview (.jpg) - A pseudocolour IO JPEG image. Available to view before processing IO data.
RGB (.tif) - A GeoTIFF giving the Red, Green and Blue waveband reflectance values of the observation at a 10m resolution.
RGB preview (.jpg) – A RGB JPEG image showing the True Colour Image (TCI) of the observation. Available to view before processing RGB data.

NUTS for the territorial level: the NUTS (Nomenclature des Unités territoriales Statistiques) classification is standardised across all EU countries to enable cross-country comparison.
NACE for the economic sector: the NACE (Statistical Classification of Economic Activities in the European Community) taxonomy is the classification of economic activities or industries in the European Union.
ISCED for educational levels: the ISCED (International Standard Classification of Education) taxonomy provides a comprehensive framework for organising education programmes and qualifications by applying uniform and internationally agreed on definitions to facilitate comparisons of education systems across countries.
ESCO (European Skills, Competences, Qualifications and Occupations) for occupations and skills: ESCO taxonomy identifies and categorises skills/competencies, qualifications, and occupations relevant for the EU labour market and education and training, in 25 European languages. It was built to provide a common language to help job seekers find jobs that match their skills, connect employment and education providers, and connect labour markets across the European Union. description:
Peaxy BlueSky Wind Data contains a comprehensive and near-real time digital footprint of wind farms, including theoretical financial profiles and Peaxy Value Score. This data contains calculated estimates for wind energy generation and revenues across 1,565 wind farms in the United States covering approximately 90% of installed base. Peaxy BlueSky Wind data is also available for Canada, Europe and Offshore locations on request. This free sample dataset lists ranking of Top100 wind farms in the Unites States based on Peaxy Value Score.
Peaxy BlueSky Wind determines which wind farms generate the most value by calculating a Peaxy Value Score for each farm. To generate the score, the system looks at real-time wind conditions for each location, applies wind turbine power curves from an extensive model library to estimate power output, and combines this with other information, including ISO region-specific electricity pricing information. The final Peaxy Value Score for each wind farm is based on wind farm revenue estimates for the last 30 days, using real-time wind and electricity pricing data for this period.
The Peaxy Value Score is used to identify the top wind farms in each state and across the U.S. The score allows comparative analyses of wind farms in the same region, highlighting the relative effectiveness of different wind turbine models operating in similar operating conditions.

title: Water Indices Maps
description:
D-CAT Water Indices Data Product Overview
Water status is an important indicator of ecosystem health. Based on the spectral signatures of liquid water and other land surface features (e.g., soil and vegetation), many water indices (WIs) have been developed to characterise the presence of liquid water. These WIs are widely used in agricultural and ecological applications including surface water body characterization, vegetation water status estimation, soil water content assessment, and wetland (e.g., paddy rice) monitoring. The features offered across different WIs mean it is important to identify the suitability of WIs for different applications.
This data product provides a time series of three different Water Index maps of areas in Argentina and Ukraine across a number of dates in 2019 and 2020. Typically, the indices provided here are used in agriculture. Each index is explained in more detail along with how they are best interpreted and how they are used in agricultural management. The three WIs provided in this sample product are: Modified Normalised Difference Water Index (MNDWI), World View Water Index (WVWI)and Normalised Difference Mud Index (NDMI). An RGB image is also provided.
The data provided here is a satellite remote sensing derived product using the European Space Agency Sentinel 2 multispectral satellite data atmospherically corrected using the Sen2cor algorithm.
 Use Cases
The range of application of WIs spreads from agricultural monitoring for crop irrigation and pasture management to forest monitoring for assessing fire risk and live fuel moisture particularly relevant in the context of climate change.
The availability of a time series of WIs therefore contributes significantly to the creation of bespoke analytics models that can improve soil health monitoring, fire risk monitoring, irrigation monitoring, crop yield prediction and biomass estimation.
 Overview - Spectral Indices
Optical imagery, i.e. pictures taken with cameras, which collect light focused by a lens, can be collected at different wavelengths within the possible range of wavelengths available (think of the colours of a rainbow).
Analysis of imagery of the same place captured at different wavelengths can reveal a lot about the content of the scene being viewed. When comparisons are made of scene content at different wavelengths, Spectral Indices are the most common form of spectral image enhancement and there are indices that support a broad range of applications, from minerals and vegetation through to soil. A Spectral Index is the name given to any numerical ratio or metric that reveals some particular aspect of information about the scene using two or more of the available images at different wavelengths.
The satellite images used by this D-CATdata product capture optical images of the same scene at 12 different wavelengths. We then apply a series of processes to those satellite images to produce these WIs. These are Spectral Indices which focus on aspects of the data which are of relevance to identifying water bodies and surface soil moisture content.
All Spectral Indices, including the three WIs offered in this sample data product, are dimensionless quantities and the file images give the WIs for each pixel imaged, i.e. the 10m2 patch of ground covered by the satellite.
 Overview - Water Indices (WIs)
WIs derived from remote sensing can be used to identify surface wetness and soil moisture, including open water. Use of remote sensing Wis for estimates of moisture is best suited to evaluating wetness at the surface. WIs have been developed to characterize vegetation water content, surface water bodies, wetland, and soil water content, based on the sensitivity of different spectral bands to water in the soil, plant, and on the surface. These WIs are widely used in drought monitoring, water body detection, wetland monitoring, and flood hazards assessment and others.
The three WIs offered in this data product have been selected for their proven applicability in monitoring soil in an agriculture context. They include: Modified Normalised Difference Water Index (MNDWI), World View Water Index (WVWI) and Normalised Difference Mud Index (NDMI). Also included is an RGB image of each satellite observation.
Each of the three WIs are now explained in more detail along with how they are best interpreted and how they are used by some practitioners to assist soil and agricultural management, monitoring and prediction.
 Modified Normalised Difference Water Index (MNDWI)
MNDWI is most typically used to map bodies of water.
It enhances open water features whilst minimising the effects of variable soil and vegetation, and so this index can also be used to give an indication of soil moisture at a surface level.
Open water has positive values on this index with larger bodies of water having high values, as opposed to built-up features which tend to have negative values along with soil and vegetation. MNDWI is therefore highly effective at distinguishing water from vegetation.
VALUE RANGE: -1 to 1
TYPICAL VALUES: Values of water bodies are larger than 0.8Soil and vegetation have values less than 0
Normalised Difference Mud Index (NDMI)
NMDI highlights muddy or shallow water pixels.
This index is not designed for larger bodies of water but instead highlights shallow regions and mixed soil / water regions (i.e. mud).
VALUE RANGE: -1 to 1
TYPICAL VALUES: Dry materials have negative values and muddy or shallow-water regions are at the other end of the scale.
World View Water Index (WVWI)
WWI highlights areas of standing water greater than one pixel in size.
This index therefore complements the other two water-related indices supplied in this sample data product enabling insights in situations ranging from little surface water to extensive bodies of water.
VALUE RANGE: -1 to 1 TYPICAL VALUES: Dry materials have negative values and water-logged regions are at the other end of the scale.
RGB
Red Green Blue (RGB) image showing the True Colour Image (TCI) of the observation.
 Metadata
Files
There are 17 unique satellite observations within this data set. 9 of these are observations of Argentina and 8 are observations of Ukraine. Observations were taken in 2019 and 2020.
There are 8 files associated with each observation:
MNDWI data (.tif) - A GeoTIFF giving Modified Normalised Difference Water Index (MNDWI) values at a 10m resolution. MNDWI is useful for showing where water is located. This can be used to differentiate features such as rivers, lakes and oceans from land. But can also show areas that have been waterlogged or lack water. Values range from -1 to 1.
MNDWI preview (.jpg) - A pseudocolour MNDWI JPEG image. Available to view before processing MNDWI data.
NDMI data (.tif) - A GeoTIFF giving Normalised Difference Mud Index (NDMI) values at a 20m resolution but has been upsampled from 20m to 10m to align with the 10m GeoTiffs. NDMI is mainly used to detect areas with mud. It can be used in conjunction with MNDWI to show where wet or dry regions are located. Values range from -1 to 1.
NDMI preview (.jpg) - A pseudocolour NDMI JPEG image. Available to view before processing NDMI data.
WVWI data (.tif) - A GeoTIFF giving World View Water Index (WVWI) values at a 60m resolution but has been upsampled from 60m to 10m to align with the 10m GeoTiffs. WVWI is similar to MNDWI in that it is useful for showing where water is located. It is also useful for detecting clouds in images. Values range from -1 to 1.
WVWI preview (.jpg) - A pseudocolour WVWI JPEG image. Available to view before processing WVWI data.
RGB (.tif) - A GeoTIFF giving the Red, Green and Blue waveband reflectance values of the observation at a 10m resolution.
RGB preview (.jpg) – A RGB JPEG image showing the True Colour Image (TCI) of the observation. Available to view before processing RGB data.

Quantum Technology Market: Overview
Quantum technology is an up-and-coming field of engineering and physics with immense potential and includes a wide range of technologically advanced devices, materials, and IT-related protocols. These technologies make use of quantum physics and mechanics to provide solutions to problems that cannot be solved by normally applied physics. Even though a lot of current technologies use quantum mechanics, there is unprecedented access to quantum technologies to their full potential by incorporating concepts like superposition and entanglement.
Quantum superposition is a founding concept of quantum mechanics and demonstrates the ability of a given quantum system to operate in different states at the same time until measured allowing for the exploration of richer and better sets of states. Quantum entanglement is the phenomenon occurring when a group of particles present close to one another and interact in a certain way where the quantum state of any particle in the given group cannot be independently described, not even when these particles are at larger distances. Quantum entanglement is what separated classic and quantum physics.

title: 2018 Baja California Mission
description:
In the summer of 2018, a Saildrone unmanned surface vehicle (USV) was launched in San Francisco to follow a course south along the US/Mexico coast toward Guadalupe Island. A coalition of 23 scientists involved in 17 projects tracked the saildrone across the highly variable California Current System with two main areas of focus: To assess the utility of Saildrone measurements for satellite sea surface temperature (SST) validation and model assimilation, and to study air-sea heat flux along dynamic frontal regions using Saildrone’s core payload of sensors and an Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler (ADCP).
The 60-day Baja Campaign cruise was the first time the Saildrone USV platform was used in comparison studies with a satellite. The Suomi NPP satellite is equipped with a Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) and provides operation data for use in global weather and climate models. The goal of this mission was to perform a three-way comparison between data collected from a Saildrone USV, the satellite, and moored buoys and research vessels along the track in a region known for complex air-land-sea dynamics.
Using a saildrone alongside existing observation platforms has the possibility of addressing gaps in spatio-temporal data collection and analysis, particularly in geographies with highly variable sea surface temperatures and upwelling. Additionally, the data collected from this mission works toward advancing research into upwelling dynamics, air-sea fluxes, and ocean fronts in an economically important part of the ocean.

title: Land Surface Temperature Maps - High Resolution
description:
D-CAT Land Surface Temperature Maps - High Resolution Data Product Overview
These 30m and 15m resolution time-series LST maps provide the detail and coverage to help identify and monitor urban heat islands, providing highly valuable environmental insights climate change and sustainability monitoring. Private data products can be tailored to offer updates of areas of interest up to every sixteen days for any city, urban and rural area.
D-CAT’s Land Surface Temperature (LST) product provides a time series of detailed temperature map files for an area. It is a satellite remote sensing derived product that takes as its input a 100m ground resolution thermal image and transforms it through pan sharpening to provide LST measurements with ground resolutions of both 15m and 30m. This example data set contains LST readings for dates in 2019 for both Prague and Singapore. The files need a geospatial viewer such as QGIS (opensource) to be viewed.
Areas with cloud, or their shadow, have been removed using a D-CAT cloud mask as these areas provide false LST readings. Areas which have been masked have been labelled as NaN (Not a Number) in both in the LST 15m data and the LST 30m data. Also provided are the cloud masks that were used. Within these GeoTIFFs, 0 represents visible land, 1 represents shadow, 2 represents thin cloud and 3 represents thick cloud.
 Use Cases
Monitoring land surface temperature provides vital insights for monitoring many land based phenomena. This product has focussed on city and urban areas, but the data can be derived for agricultural and wildland.
For the urban use case, with increased urbanisation, natural surfaces are being replaced by artificial ones with different thermal properties creating changes in the local climate. This LST product offers a powerful time-series remote sensing derived data product for the study of the urban environment.  
This new LST insight is a huge boost for hot cities of the world where city planners, architects and developers are actively formulating plans to combat climate change. They need to ensure their cities remain attractive places to live and work. This new product offers planners, architects, developers and the public access to reliable, accurate land surface temperature measurements across the city and metropolitan area and will help all in their goal of achieving better informed planning and development decisions.  
These high-resolution temperature map complement the more conventional temperature data that are typically gathered by a network of urban meteorological stations. Such urban networks of meteorological stations may not always be as complete as desirable and are not always evenly distributed spatially across a city. Consequently, some large areas may remain without coverage. D-CAT’s Smart City LST product offers a step change in providing additional high value data for the cost-effective identification and monitoring of urban heat islands at the city and urban level.  
The LST product also creates the potential for wider, inter agency collaboration across a city too. For example, an innovative water company in Australia used this LST data to explore new techniques to cool the city during times of extreme thermal stress in the summer months. One of the most promising approaches they identified in this ground-breaking research was the recognition that spraying water on urban greenery, such as parks and sports fields, reduced the temperature of inner city’s business district by as much as 2 degrees celsius.

title: Financial Results Score
description:
Overview
Using information from the past three years' fiscal results, financial results score is calculated. For each sales, operating income, and net income, the degree of upswing or downswing from the target level is evaluated on a five-point scale based on the following criteria. The average value of these three is used as the final financial results score. Target levels are set as follows.
First, the annual target level is set at the company's most recent forecast for the current fiscal year.
The average progress rate over the past three years at the end of the relevant quarter is determined, and the annual target level multiplied by the average progress rate is set as the target level.
However, if the company's forecast for the quarter exists, that value shall be used as the target level. For companies that have not published their company forecasts, we use NA value. The five-point scale of each score based on the following criteria.

The global imaging photometers market is projected to be US$ 35.4 Mn in 2018 to reach US$ 50.8 Mn by 2021 at a CAGR of 3.7%.
Imaging photometer 
is an instrument used for measuring luminous intensity of the light source, by comparing it with the standard source. In photometry, visual photometer observer sees a field illuminated alternately from two sources which are compared. Once flicker sensation disappears – the intensity of the test source is concluded by comparing it with the standard source. In other terms, imaging photometer refers to an instrument used for the measurement of light intensity and understanding the optical properties of surface and solutions. Imaging photometers interpret brightness at spatial and angular distribution just the way humans do and are adaptable to applications requiring human visual interpretation of light at variable distances and angles. Imaging photometers are fast, reliable and accurate, particularly for large production lines. In addition, imaging photometry technique provides objective information that can be evaluated, compared and shared.
Increased investments in R&D for advanced visualization systems by government and private authorities are providing significant growth to the imaging photometers market. It acts as the nerve center, managing and optimizing operations in real-time, enhancing efficiency, and ensuring safety protocols. DCS plays a pivotal role in industries such as manufacturing, energy, oil and gas, and pharmaceuticals, where intricate processes demand precision and reliability in control.
Catalyzing Innovation: The surge in investments within the manufacturing and processing industry is a driving force behind the flourishing Distributed Control System (DCS) market. As the manufacturing sector expands, there is an escalating demand for advanced control systems that can optimize production processes and enhance overall efficiency. Technological advancements, particularly in the realms of the Internet of Things (IoT) and artificial intelligence (AI), are elevating DCS systems to unprecedented levels of power and capability, further fueling demand.
These factors are compelling companies to enhance their operations to stay competitive in the global marketplace. For instance, Mitsubishi Electric India's launch of the GOC43 in November 2020 exemplifies this trend. This indigenous human-machine interface (HMI) controller, compatible with most automation systems including DCS, was designed to withstand harsh industrial environments. Its applications span across various industries, including manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, HVAC, and automotive, showcasing the adaptability and relevance of DCS in diverse industrial settings.
Industry 4.0 Adoption: n the era of Industry 4.0, characterized by the integration of digital technologies into industrial processes, DCS plays a crucial role in enhancing operational efficiency and connectivity. The seamless integration of DCS with emerging technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), and advanced analytics propels industries towards smart automation. As businesses increasingly embrace Industry 4.0 principles, the demand for sophisticated DCS solutions rises, reflecting a symbiotic relationship between technological innovation and the evolution of the DCS market.
Demand for Energy-Efficient Solutions: In today's dynamic energy landscape, the growing consumer preference for clean and renewable energy sources is steering a significant expansion in the industry. A pivotal player in this transformation is the Distributed Control System (DCS), which assumes a critical role in the management of electricity generated from renewable sources like wind, solar, and hydropower. The increasing adoption of renewable energy leads to a more decentralized and intricate power grid, underscoring the essential role of DCS in seamlessly integrating and managing these diverse energy sources.
DCS is indispensable for monitoring and controlling the flow of electricity from various sources, ensuring optimal utilization of energy storage systems. The mounting demand for renewable energy is a major catalyst propelling the growth of distributed control systems in the energy sector. Luminate Current & Historical Television dataset includes over 80,000 TV series and programs across broadcast, cable and first run syndication from the 1999-2000 season to the present season. It is quite simply the gold standard of television program metadata across the US, UK, and Canada.

title: US TV Streaming Exclusives - Daily News Coverage (Sample for Trial)
description:
Meltwater has extensive experience in aggregating content across news and social media for over 32,000 clients globally. Over 500 million new documents are processed daily and enriched using best-in-class natural language processing. Meltwater Packaged Data Products are easy to consume, with rich metadata and are designed to provide AWS Data Exchange customers in the Media & Entertainment industry with insights to support specific use cases.
As the streaming wars heat up in the US, this timely dataset will help production companies, licensors, and the streaming platforms themselves to track news coverage for many of the flagship shows promoted by the major streaming platforms. This dataset offers a 1-week sample.
Over 80 shows are tracked, each of which is mapped to the streaming service it is featured on.
Netflix Exclusives include Stranger Things, BoJack Horseman and Black Mirror Disney Plus Exclusives include The Mandalorian, Forky Asks A Question, Monsters at Work and High School Musical: The Musical: The Series, Prime Video Exclusives include The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel, The Expanse,Jack Ryan, Mr Robot and Carnival Row Apple TV Plus Exclusives include Dickinson, The Morning Show, For All Mankind and Oprah’s Book Club Notes on the data structure:

Entity level sentiment detection provides for a more accurate and reliable measure than document level sentiment. Over 30 values are provided for each row of data.

description:

The Onclusive Social Media Counts Sample dataset consists of article urls published in a given time period (2019/10/1 - 2019/10/5) and the number of Facebook likes each article received.
Files are JSONL and gzipped, Athena-compatible
field type description example
url string canonical url of article "https://foo.com/news/2019/10/some-article"
fb_likes int number of Facebook likes 479
date string date of article publication "2019-10-01"
Steps to access social counts data via Amazon Athena:
Download the data set to your S3 bucket.
Set all required IAM permissions for Athena.
You can run following DDL to create Athena Table.
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE <table_name> (
url string,
facebook_likes int,
date string
)
ROW FORMAT SERDE 'org.openx.data.jsonserde.JsonSerDe'
LOCATION '<Your S3 Bucket>';
Sample Queries:
SELECT date, count(*)
FROM <table_name>
GROUP BY date
LIMIT 10; 
SELECT *
FROM <table_name>
LIMIT 10;
 -- Top 10 URL with most facebook likes --
SELECT url, sum(facebook_likes) AS facebook_likes
FROM <table_name>
WHERE date >= 'from_date'
AND date <  'to_date'
GROUP BY url
ORDER BY facebook_likes DESC
LIMIT 10;

Global Events Industry Market
Events Industry Market: Overview
According to Custom Market Insights (CMI), The Events Industry Market 
size was estimated at USD 1,190.4 Billion in 2022 and is expected to hit around USD 1,752.9 Billion by 2032, poised to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 12% from 2023 to 2032.
The events industry market refers to the sector encompassing the planning, organization, and management of various types of events. It includes a wide range of events such as conferences, trade shows, exhibitions, corporate meetings, weddings, music concerts, sports events, festivals, and more.
The market encompasses multiple segments, including event planning and management services, venue management, event technology solutions, event marketing and promotion, event registration and ticketing services, and other related services. The events industry market serves as a platform for individuals, organizations, and businesses to host events that bring people together for various purposes, such as networking, knowledge sharing, entertainment, celebration, product launches, and business transactions.
The market involves event organizers, event planners, event technology providers, venue operators, suppliers, exhibitors, sponsors, and attendees. The events industry market is driven by factors such as increasing demand for unique experiences, the need for effective communication and networking, business expansion opportunities, and the desire for entertainment and leisure activities. It plays a vital role in sectors such as business, tourism, hospitality, entertainment, and marketing.
The industry is characterized by constant innovation and adaptation to changing trends and technologies. In recent years, there has been a significant shift towards virtual and hybrid events, driven by advancements in event technology and the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. Virtual events allow for remote participation and engagement, while hybrid events combine in-person and virtual elements.

Events Industry Market: Growth Drivers
Evolving Consumer Expectations: Consumer expectations in the events industry are continuously evolving. Attendees seek unique and immersive experiences, personalized interactions, and meaningful engagement. Event organizers need to innovate and incorporate elements like technology integration, experiential marketing, and customization to meet these changing expectations.
Digital Transformation: Digital transformation has significantly impacted the events industry. Online ticketing platforms, event management software, virtual and hybrid event solutions, and social media promotion have reshaped the way events are planned, executed, and experienced. Embracing digital tools and platforms is crucial for event organizers to enhance efficiency, reach wider audiences, and deliver engaging experiences.
Rise of Experiential Events: Experiential events have gained prominence in the industry. Attendees seek immersive and memorable experiences that go beyond traditional event formats. Event organizers are focusing on incorporating interactive elements, unique themes, live performances, and sensory experiences to create lasting impressions and increase attendee satisfaction.
Sustainability and Social Responsibility: Environmental sustainability and social responsibility have become significant considerations in the events industry. Event organizers are adopting sustainable practices, reducing waste, minimizing carbon footprints, and promoting ethical sourcing. Incorporating social impact initiatives and supporting local communities are also key factors in event planning and execution.
Integration of Technology: Technology plays a crucial role in enhancing event experiences. Event organizers are leveraging technologies like event apps, live streaming, augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance engagement, provide personalized experiences, and facilitate seamless event execution.

Events Industry Market: Regional Analysis
North America: North America holds a significant share of the events industry market. The region is known for hosting a wide range of events, including trade shows, conferences, music festivals, and sports events. Major cities like New York, Las Vegas, and Los Angeles serve as prominent event destinations. The presence of a large number of corporations, strong infrastructure, and high consumer spending contributes to the growth of the events industry in this region.
Europe: Europe is another key region in the events industry market. Countries such as the UK, Germany, France, and Spain are known for hosting major international events, conferences, and exhibitions. The region benefits from a rich cultural heritage, historical venues, and a strong emphasis on business networking events. Additionally, popular music festivals and sporting events draw large crowds and contribute to the overall growth of the events industry in Europe.
Asia Pacific: The Asia Pacific region is experiencing rapid growth in the events industry. Countries like China, Japan, India, and Singapore are emerging as key event destinations. Rising disposable incomes, urbanization, and increasing interest in experiential events contribute to the growth of the market in this region. Additionally, the growing popularity of corporate events, trade shows, and technology conferences in countries like China and India drives market expansion.
Latin America: Latin America offers significant growth potential in the events industry market. Brazil, Mexico, and Argentina are the major contributors to this region. Cultural festivals, music events, and sports tournaments like the FIFA World Cup and Copa America attract both domestic and international attendees. The region’s vibrant culture, scenic locations, and growing tourism industry contribute to the development of the events industry.
Middle East and Africa: The Middle East and Africa region are witnessing increased investments in the events industry. Dubai, Abu Dhabi, and Doha are popular event destinations known for hosting international conferences, exhibitions, and sports events. The region’s focus on infrastructure development, business tourism, and the rise of mega-events like World Expos contribute to the growth of the events industry.
